title: The Khokhars Rise on the Jhelum

title_i18n.en: The Khokhars Rise on the Jhelum

subtitle: Revolt on the Salt Range
era: Khokhar revolt and Ghurid crisis, 1204-1206 CE
region: Punjab, Jhelum river and Dhamiak in the Salt Range
moral: A source problem can be as important as a battlefield.

sources.citation: Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, c. 1260 CE
sources.note: Delhi Sultanate insider source close to the Ghurid world.

sources.citation: Ibn al-Athir, Al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, c. 1231 CE; Ferishta, Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi, c. 1606 CE
sources.note: Independent near-contemporary account and much later Persian synthesis.

sources.citation: A.B.M. Habibullah, The Foundation of Muslim Rule in India (1961); Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)
sources.note: Modern discussion of the revolt, massacre and transition to Delhi rule.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of the Salt Range over the Jhelum, storm clouds gathering

dialogue.text: On the cliffs of the Jhelum, Raisal and Bhikan Khokhar defied Muhammad of Ghor—and left behind not one story, but a tangle of chronicles and legend.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot over map-like Punjab, tracing routes between Ghazni, Lahore, and Multan

dialogue.text: In the early 1200s, the power of Muhammad of Ghor flowed through the roads of the Punjab—thin lines of supply binding Ghazni to Lahore and the Ganges plain.

panels.shot: medium wide of a busy road near Lahore, caravans and soldiers mingling

dialogue.text: Victories at Tarain and Chandawar had opened north India, but they also stretched Ghurid power thin, its armies and treasures forever on the move.

panels.shot: low-angle medium of Raisal and Bhikan watching a distant convoy from a wooded ridge

dialogue.text: In the hills above these roads lived the Khokhars—tribal chiefs of the Salt Range, fierce horsemen and raiders who had long guarded and taxed the passes.

panels.shot: tight medium on a Khokhar council circle by firelight

dialogue.speaker: Bhikan
dialogue.text: They take our hills for their road. Let them learn these hills bite.

panels.shot: dynamic wide of an ambush in a narrow defile, viewed from above

dialogue.text: Around 1204, the chronicles say, the Khokhars rose. They blocked the passes, struck at caravans, and cut the veins that fed Lahore and Ghazni.

panels.shot: close-up on a Ghurid messenger spurring his horse, dust flying

dialogue.text: In Lahore, word came like a wound. Muhammad’s lieutenants sent urgent messages west: the Punjab roads were no longer safe.

panels.shot: regal interior medium of Muhammad of Ghor seated in council in Ghazni (Muhammad unseen, implied by throne and courtiers)

dialogue.text: Far to the west, in Ghazni, Muhammad of Ghor listened. To lose the Punjab roads was to lose the bridge to his Indian conquests.

panels.shot: long shot of a Ghurid army column leaving Ghazni, mountains in background

dialogue.text: So he came in person. The sources agree: in 1206, Muhammad marched east against the Khokhar revolt on the Jhelum.

panels.shot: wide shot of opposing forces facing off near the Jhelum, river glinting between them

dialogue.text: On the banks of the Jhelum, the two worlds met—organized imperial host below, hill fighters above, each testing who truly held the passage.

panels.shot: medium close on Raisal drawing his bow, grim focus

dialogue.speaker: Raisal
dialogue.text: For every pass they take, we take a man.

panels.shot: chaotic mid-wide of the battlefield, dust and confusion, no graphic violence

dialogue.text: The chroniclers give no neat numbers, only hard words: a revolt, bitter fighting, then a crushing of the Khokhars by the sultan’s army.

panels.shot: somber wide of a subdued Khokhar encampment under Ghurid guard

dialogue.text: Minhaj and Ibn al-Athir record the aftermath: many Khokhars killed, others taken as captives, with talk of forced conversion and enslavement in the Persian tradition.

panels.shot: close-up on a Ghurid officer dictating to a scribe, scroll partially unrolled

dialogue.text: These accounts were written from the victors’ halls, but they agree: the revolt was broken by heavy, punitive violence.

panels.shot: medium of Muhammad’s camp at Dhamiak by night, tents around a central pavilion

dialogue.text: With the roads reopened, Muhammad of Ghor turned homeward. At a place called Dhamiak, near the Salt Range, he camped for the night.

panels.shot: tense close-up on a shadowed figure entering the royal pavilion flap

dialogue.text: Then the chronicles fall into shadow. Minhaj and Ibn al-Athir relate that assassins stole into the sultan’s tent at Dhamiak.

panels.shot: interior silhouette shot of confusion in the pavilion, lamp overturned

dialogue.text: They name them Ismaili or Batini killers, part of a wider web of secret foes that stalked rulers from Iran to India.

panels.shot: wide dawn shot of the camp in disarray, banners lowered

dialogue.text: By morning, Muhammad of Ghor was dead. The road-clearing conqueror of the Khokhars would never return to Ghazni or Delhi.

panels.shot: split-scene style wide: on one side a Persian court historian writing; on the other, Khokhar warriors around a hill fire

dialogue.text: Later, Ferishta would echo a different voice—that the Khokhars, not hidden sectaries, avenged their dead upon their conqueror.

panels.shot: medium close on an open manuscript showing two marginal notes in different hands

dialogue.text: Modern historians note the pattern: agreement on the revolt, its brutal suppression, and the sultan’s death—disagreement on who dealt the final blow.

panels.shot: wide contemplative shot of Raisal and Bhikan’s silhouettes against the Salt Range, years later feel

dialogue.text: Between the Khokhar hills and the Dhamiak plain, we are left with roads, ruins, and rival chronicles—a reminder that in history, the battle is only half the story, the sources the other half.
